title: VPC on-prem troubleshooting cheat sheet (terraform & upgrades)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact troubleshooting cheat sheet and smoke-test checklist for VPC / on-prem Redwood Private deployments. It focuses on the most common install/runtime failures we hit during installs and upgrades and includes quick Terraform module notes and a safe upgrade checklist. Keep this open during dry-runs or first-hour incidents.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes):
- Confirm scope: Is this single-host on-prem, multi-node k8s, or a VPC-connected deployment?
- Check control-plane & agent health: kubectl get nodes | kubectl get pods -n redwood || systemctl status redwood-agent
- Confirm network reachability: ping to registry/storage endpoints, curl health endpoints (http://<node-ip>:8080/health) and traceroute if network failure is suspected.
- Check tfstate/locking: is remote state accessible? terraform plan errors often indicate backend access issues.

Common install failures, symptoms, and quick fixes:
1) Model fetch / artifact pull failures Symptom: service logs show 404/403 from S3-compatible endpoint OR long hanging model download and eventual timeout.
Root causes: bad endpoint URL, credentials rotated, firewall blocking egress, S3 sig/version mismatch, wrong bucket region.
Quick fixes:
- curl -I <artifact-url> from node to verify reachability and creds.
- Check env vars (MODEL_STORE_URL, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY).
- If using S3-compatible storage, verify path-style vs virtual-host-style and TLS.
- Temporarily open egress to confirm firewall is culprit.

2) Container runtime / GPU not available Symptom: model worker fails to start, logs: "no CUDA devices found" or nvidia-smi absent/fails.
Root causes: wrong NVIDIA driver, missing nvidia-container-toolkit, kernel module not loaded, incompatible driver vs CUDA.
Quick fixes:
- Run nvidia-smi; check kernel modules with lsmod | grep nvidia.
- If using containerd, ensure nvidia-container-toolkit + containerd integration configured.
- For nodes with GPUs, confirm drivers installed via package manager or vendor installer, reboot if required.

3) OOMs during model load or inference Symptom: worker restarted, OOMKilled in pod events, model load fails.
Root causes: under-provisioned node memory, incorrect resource limits, quantization/precision mismatch.
Quick fixes:
- kubectl describe pod to see OOMKilled.
- Increase container memory limits or reduce model batch-size.
- Consider switching to a quantized model build if memory constrained.

4) TLS/cert validation errors for control plane Symptom: agents cannot register, TLS handshake failures in logs.
Root causes: expired certs, wrong SANs for internal DNS, clock skew.
Quick fixes:
- Check cert expiry openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -dates.
- Confirm node time sync (chronyd/ntpd).
- If SAN mismatch, re-issue certs with correct hostnames; use short-term workaround with allow-insecure-connection only during maintenance.

5) DNS / VPC routing issues Symptom: services can’t reach each other by hostname; intermittent timeouts.
Root causes: misconfigured VPC route tables, improper DNS host zones, MTU mismatch with tunnels (e.g., GRE/VPN).
Quick fixes:
- nslookup / dig from affected pod/node.
- Check VPC route tables and peering rules.
- Lower MTU on host tunnel interfaces to 1400 as test.

Terraform module notes (common gotchas & tips):
- Provider & module pinning: Always pin provider versions and module tags in production modules (aws, kubernetes, helm, local backend). Example: source = "git::https://...//modules/private-deploy?ref=v1.4.2".
- Remote state & locking: Ensure state backend (S3 + DynamoDB, or GCS) is reachable from maintenance workstation. terraform init will fail silently on credentials issues.
- Workspaces vs envs: Prefer separate tfstate buckets per environment; avoid multi-env single workspace unless intentional.
- lifecycle.ignore_changes: Use sparingly when provider recreations are noisy (e.g., ignore changes to autoscaler settings managed externally). Document rationale in module variables.
- Importing existing infra: Use terraform import for resources created by install scripts. Keep an import-playbook with exact resource IDs and provider aliases.
- Plan review: Always run terraform plan with -out and check diffs for replacements that cause downtime ("-/+" means replace).
- State drift & driftsafe apply: For resources that may be modified by external processes (e.g., routing tables), add pre-checks to detect unexpected drift before apply.

Upgrade / patch plan (safe rollout checklist):
Pre-upgrade (1–3 days out):
- Create backups: snapshot model storage, DB backups, and take tfstate snapshot (copy bucket object). - Open a smoke-test incident channel and notify stakeholders. - Freeze non-essential deploys and document last-known-good artifact versions.

Day-of checklist (execute during maintenance window):
1. Validate baseline metrics: error rate, latency, inbound rate, GPU utilization.
2. Run pre-upgrade smoke-tests (see Smoke-test section). Save outputs and baselines.
3. terraform plan -> review for resource replacement; abort if control-plane resources will be replaced unexpectedly.
4. Apply to a canary subset (one node/pool or single AZ): terraform apply -target=module.canary or apply helm chart to canary namespace.
5. Run quick canary smoke-tests and monitor logs & metrics for 15–30 minutes.
6. If canary passes, proceed with staged rollout (25% -> 50% -> 100%).
7. If failure: run rollback steps (helm rollback or restore from snapshot), then escalate.

Rollback playbook (fast):
- If terraform changed infra (resource replaced): use terraform state rollback snapshot and re-apply last-known-good plan. - If application/config change: helm rollback <release> <REV> or redeploy previous container image tag. - If model artifacts corrupted: restore from snapshot and restart workers.

Smoke-test checklist (automated/tests to run after install/upgrade):
- Health endpoint: GET /health -> must return 200 and minimal latency (<200ms). - Auth check: token introspection / auth flow with customer Id.
- Model load: request load of small model and large model; record load times and memory usage.
- Quick generation: run n=10 short inferences (<=64 tokens) and assert no errors and response time within SLO.
- Embedding test: submit batch of 5 texts, assert vector dims correct and no NaNs.
- Streaming test: open a streaming request and verify partial tokens arrive within latency budget.
- GPU check: run a short gpu-stress test that does a forward pass and confirm GPU util > 10% and no ECC errors in dmesg.
- Persistence & artifacts: upload a small artifact and confirm retrieval via signed URL.
- TF plan idempotency: run terraform plan twice — second run should be no-op.

Commands & quick snippets:
- View k8s events for failing pods: kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> --previous; kubectl -n redwood describe pod <pod>
- Check driver: sudo nvidia-smi || sudo dmesg | tail -n 50
- Check model registry access: curl -v "${MODEL_STORE_URL}/model.tgz" -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ARTIFACT_TOKEN}"
- Check cert expiry: openssl x509 -in /etc/redwood/certs/server.pem -noout -dates
- Terraform plan with out: terraform plan -out upgrade.plan && terraform show -json upgrade.plan | jq '.'

Observability signals to watch during a rollout:
- Increased 5xx rate from API or internal RPCs.
- Sudden spike in model load latencies or re-loads (indicates eviction/OOM).
- Node-level kernel messages (OOM killer, GPU ECC, driver panics).
- Increased reattempts to artifact store (sign of networking or credential issue).

Notes & lessons learned (common human errors):
- Cutting over provider versions without testing local changes to module outputs causes resource replacements.
- Forgetting to update kubelet/containerd config for new nvidia toolkit version (results in "no devices").
- Assuming identical MTU across VPNs — leads to random packet drops for large responses.

What to add to infra runbooks (action items):
- Document exact steps to verify tfstate copy & restore.
- Keep a list of last-known-good container images & model hashes.
- Provide a canonical quick-check script (bash) that runs baseline smoke-tests and prints PASS/FAIL.

Appendix: short quick-check script outline (to paste into maintenance shell)
- curl http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1
- python3 -c "from redwood_client import Client; c=Client(); print(c.generate('hi'))" || exit 2
- nvidia-smi || echo 'no-gpu'
- terraform plan -no-color || echo 'tf-plan-failed'

If you add to this doc, include a short note at top with date and what was changed. Preserve short commands; prefer links to full runbooks rather than duplicating long procedures.

End of cheat sheet.
